title: The Weather of Room 214
premise: Wendell Montrose has spent thirty years as a night librarian, cataloging other people's overdue lives while keeping their own family history in a shoebox of unsent letters. When the childhood house at 214 Marrow Street goes up for auction, Wendell's estranged siblings converge to sell it—and to finally decide what to do about their mother, whose dementia is erasing the one secret the family was built to protect: what happened the night their father left. As the auction nears and their mother's memory thins to gauze, Wendell must choose between preserving the family's careful arrangement of silences and speaking the truth that might let all of them be loved as they actually are. The novel ends not with the house sold but with Wendell reading the letters aloud to their mother, who cannot hold the memory but can still feel its warmth—and with the family, imperfectly, staying.
about_author: Tamsin Amberdale is a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging private letters in a university special collections before turning to fiction. She writes at night, in libraries, about the people cities forget to put to bed.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Wendell's POV. A night shift at the Halloway Free Library introduces Wendell's habit of writing letters they never send, filed in a shoebox. A letter from a lawyer about 214 Marrow Street arrives in the returns bin. Beat: quiet dread dressed as routine.

chapters.title: A House Is Just a Delayed Letter
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell visits the boarded-up childhood home, finding their own height marks on a doorframe and their mother's handwriting on the pantry wall. The auction date is set for six weeks out. Beat: the past asserting itself as physical fact.

chapters.title: The Sibling Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Brother Caspian calls with logistics and zero feeling; sister Odile texts only in practical fragments. Wendell realizes the family communicates exclusively in arrangements, never in sentences. Beat: loneliness inside a full family.

chapters.title: What the Night Shift Knows
chapters.summary: Library patron Marisol's POV, briefly. A homeless regular who sleeps in the reading room tells Wendell that libraries are where people hide in plain sight—mirroring what Wendell has done for decades. Beat: being seen by a stranger.

chapters.title: Mother, Reduced to a Weather Report
chapters.summary: Wendell visits their mother, Vera, at Fernwood Care, where she mistakes Wendell for her late husband. Vera speaks in fragments about 'the night of the rain,' the family's forbidden subject. Beat: tenderness sharpened by evasion.

chapters.title: Caspian's Ledger
chapters.summary: Caspian's POV. At a family meeting in a diner, Caspian presents the auction plan like a balance sheet and shuts down Wendell's suggestion to ask Vera about their father. Beat: the machinery of silence, well-oiled.

chapters.title: Odile's Perfect Distance
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile, who lives two time zones away and calls it freedom, admits in interior monologue that her marriage is another Marrow Street—arranged around a silence. Beat: complicity revealed as its own kind of wound.

chapters.title: The Shoebox, Opened
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell rereads thirty years of unsent letters and finds the first one, written at age eleven, the night their father left. The memory arrives with rain, a broken window, and something Wendell has never let themselves finish remembering. Beat: the past knocking.

chapters.title: An Appraisal of Everything
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. An estate appraiser catalogs the house's objects, and Wendell watches their childhood priced line by line—a lamp at forty dollars, their mother's wedding dress unsellable. Beat: grief measured in inventory, Wendell's native language failing them.

chapters.title: The Rain, Again
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, flashback woven into present. Half the memory returns: the father's suitcase, the mother standing in the doorway, and Wendell—eleven years old—saying something that made everyone rearrange their lives around it. The sentence itself stays missing. Beat: dread of one's own words.

chapters.title: Marisol's Overdue Book
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol returns a book twenty years overdue and asks Wendell why they never left the night shift. Wendell answers honestly for the first time: 'Because no one looks for you at night.' Beat: confession as rehearsal.

chapters.title: Caspian Breaks Something
chapters.summary: Caspian's POV. Clearing the garage, Caspian smashes their father's workbench and confesses to Wendell that he saw their father once, years later, and said nothing. Beat: the silence shown to be load-bearing for everyone.

chapters.title: Odile Comes Home Early
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile arrives unannounced, her marriage quietly ended, and sleeps in her childhood bedroom. She and Wendell almost speak the truth to each other and instead organize the linen closet. Beat: intimacy defeated by habit.

chapters.title: What Vera Still Has
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Vera has a lucid hour and asks Wendell directly, 'Did you ever tell them what you told me?' Wendell lies. Vera, even diminished, knows. Beat: the mother as keeper of the secret she's losing.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalog
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The auction catalog arrives; the house and its contents are photographed, described, and made strange. Wendell finds their father listed as 'male, departed' in a genealogical note. Beat: erasure formalized, anger kindling.

chapters.title: Three Siblings, One Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Rotating POV across all three siblings in one scene. In the house, they find their father's locked desk drawer, and each privately wants it opened and dreads it. They agree, unanimously, to leave it sealed for the auction. Beat: the family's arrangement reasserting itself one last time.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Auction
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell breaks into their own childhood home, sits on the kitchen floor, and finally finishes the memory: they told their father that if he left, they would tell everyone why—and then, out of fear, told their mother a version that made her carry the blame. Beat: the missing sentence found, devastating in its smallness.

chapters.title: Auction
chapters.summary: All three siblings' POVs interwoven. At the auction, the drawer is sold unopened to a stranger. Caspian bids on nothing; Odile leaves mid-lot; Wendell watches strangers carry the house away. Beat: public loss forcing private reckoning.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell takes the shoebox to Fernwood and reads the unsent letters to Vera, including the truth of that night. Vera doesn't retain it, but she takes Wendell's hand and says, 'There you are.' Beat: the climax—truth spoken, love received without memory.

chapters.title: Caspian's Letter
chapters.summary: Caspian's POV. Caspian writes his first letter in forty years—to the father's forwarding address, returned undeliverable—and mails it anyway. He tells Wendell he's going to therapy, in the least therapy-friendly sentence ever constructed. Beat: the silence cracking in the sibling who guarded it hardest.

chapters.title: Odile Stays the Night
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile stays in the city, gets a small apartment, and begins telling the truth in increments—first to Wendell, then to her adult daughter. Beat: identity rebuilt from the wreckage of duty.

chapters.title: The Weather of Room 214
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Wendell keeps the night shift but leaves the library window open to the weather, sends one letter, and visits Vera, who greets them as a kind stranger every time—and every time, Wendell introduces themselves anyway. Beat: resolution—love chosen daily, without the shelter of silence.
